title: Semi-Supervised Hypothesis Testing by Betting on Predictions
claim: Our betting-based test gains power over baselines across unlabeled-data regimes, even when predictions are weak or data is scarce.
layout: 4 line-plot panels in a row, shared legend on top
description: A single horizontal strip of four line plots labeled (a) to (d), with one shared legend across the top. Every panel has Step (0 to 500) on the x-axis and statistical Power (0 to 1) on the y-axis. Five colored curves with markers and light shaded confidence bands are shown: blue circles for 'Baselines with Ours', orange squares for 'Baselines w/o Ours', red crosses for 'Only Ours', green triangles for e_LR^Y, and purple triangles for e_LR^X. The panels run from weak to strong unlabeled-data signal. In (a), blue ends highest at about 0.77. In (b), blue stays on top at about 0.88. In (c), the curves climb toward about 0.95. In (d), most curves saturate near 1.0 early, the red curve rises later, and green lags. The eye goes first to the blue curve.
caption: Simulation results for the label shift setting. In all settings, the signal strength of the labeled data is fixed and the signal strength of the unlabeled data varies between plots: (a) weak (N = 30, low correlation), (b) medium (N = 135, low correlation), (c) medium-high (N = 30, high correlation), (d) strong (N = 135, high correlation).
abstract: We introduce a testing-by-betting framework that leverages predictions on unlabeled data to enhance the power of sequential hypothesis testing. Given limited samples from the joint distribution of $(X,Y)$, and additional unlabeled samples from the marginal of $X$, we ask how unlabeled data can be used to hypothesize about the distribution of $Y$, and the conditional distribution of $Y\mid X$. We introduce an e-statistic and use it to construct a sequential test. Under standard distributional assumptions -- label shift or concept shift -- we establish that the test is anytime valid. Furthermore, we show that for binary data, the e-statistic has non-trivial power. Crucially, our approach retains these properties even when the underlying predictions are inaccurate. Through simulations and applications to large language models evaluation, we demonstrate power gains over baseline approaches, including prediction-powered inference. These gains persist even with relatively limited unlabeled data and when predictions have low accuracy due to weak correlation between $X$ and $Y$.
